name: Inchworm
description: The inchworm is a dynamic warm-up and functional movement exercise in which the athlete bends forward to place the hands on the floor and walks the hands out to a push-up plank position, then walks the feet back toward the hands to return upright. It simultaneously provides a hamstring stretch during the foot-walk phase, shoulder and chest warm-up in the plank phase, and an optional push-up for further activation. The inchworm is a highly efficient all-in-one mobility and activation drill used globally as a warm-up.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright with feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Adequate floor space for the walk-out length.
steps: Step 1: Stand upright, then hinge forward at the hips and bend the knees slightly to place both hands on the floor.
Step 2: Walk the hands forward — step by step — until arriving in a full push-up plank position.
Step 3: Optional: perform one push-up in the plank position.
Step 4: Walk the feet toward the hands in small steps, keeping the legs as straight as hamstring flexibility allows.
Step 5: Arrive in a standing position and repeat for the prescribed number of reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you walk out. Inhale as you walk feet back in.
common_mistakes: Bending the knees excessively during the foot-walk phase — the hamstring stretch is the goal of that phase
Letting the hips sag in the plank position
Rushing — the inchworm is a quality movement, not a speed exercise
safety_considerations: Limited hamstring flexibility will cause excessive knee bend — this is fine initially, improve over time.
Wrist discomfort in the plank position — warm up wrists before.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk hands as far as a full plank. Walk feet as close to hands as hamstring flexibility allows with minimal knee bend.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 5–10 reps as a warm-up. Slow and deliberate.
coaching_cues: Walk the feet in — feel the hamstring stretch
